az_granite_mountain.blurb: A granite massif west of Prescott in central Arizona, set in a wilderness unit of Prescott National Forest. The southwest face is a sheer cliff roughly 500 feet high, and the pale, fine-grained granite is split by cracks and natural lines. Trad is the main event, with a smaller supply of top-rope and sport lines and a few boulders. Grades start easy and reach the low 5.13s, but most climbs fall between 5.8 and 5.12, with a lot of 5.10 and 5.11. The crowds tend to stay thin. The climbing is divided into sections: the Middle Section is the largest, then the Right Section and Swamp Slabs, with the Granite Basin Crags as a separate cluster nearby. Descents combine scrambling with rappels.

ca_bear_valley.blurb: Bear Valley sits along State Highway 4, the Ebbets Pass Highway, at around 7,100 feet. This is bouldering country almost entirely, spread over small, remote pockets rather than one big venue, with a single trad line and a single sport line as the only exceptions. Problems skew easy: V0 is the most common grade, with plenty of V1 to V3 and only a handful above V4. Near the Stanislaus River and at Spicer Reservoir the boulders are granite. Along the river they range from small warm-up blocks to larger faces, some on the far bank, while Spicer's are mostly short and sit beside the road, with extra rock showing along the shoreline when the water is low. Hell's Kitchen is another cluster.

ut_ogden_boulder_field.blurb: A big hillside of boulders on Ogden's East Bench, in the Wasatch Range at roughly 5,100 feet. The rock is quartzite, and the climbing is nearly all bouldering, with just a lone trad line. Many boulders can be seen from the streets at the top of town, so it is easy to scout. Problems begin at V0 and cluster between V0 and V6, with a few V7 and V8 and a small group of V11s for the strongest. The Lower Boulder Field holds the most problems; the Upper Boulder Field lies north up Taylor's Canyon, and the Patriot Crack Area sits uphill, north of the lower field.

az_isolation_canyon.blurb: A quartzite canyon carved by Pine Creek just outside the town of Pine in central Arizona, within Tonto National Forest, at about 5,200 feet. The cliffs run from roughly 40 to 300 feet, with routes of one to four pitches on very hard, near-vertical, well-featured rock that wears a coat of colorful lichen. Trad and sport both have a strong presence, trad a little more so, plus a handful of boulder problems. Grades run from easy 5th class to 5.12, but the bulk sit between 5.8 and 5.11, with 5.10 and 5.11 the most common. The Main Wall is divided into North, Center and South sections, and other walls include Finktion Wall, Spaghetti Western Wall and Winter Wall.

co_lory_state_park.blurb: A state park on the west side of Fort Collins, near the northwest end of Horsetooth Reservoir, at about 5,600 feet. Bouldering makes up most of the climbing, with smaller helpings of sport and trad and a stray top rope. Boulder problems stretch from V0 to V12 with a broad spread of moderates, while the routes run from 5.7 to 5.12. Arthur's Rock is the heart of it: a mixed granite conglomerate where the climbing is fingery, with small edges, gritty slopers and the odd knob, and quality that varies a lot. Its sunny, south-facing cliff climbs well in winter, spring and fall, but summer is generally too hot. Newly developed sandstone boulders are found on the east side of the park, along with Eltuck Bay, Mill Creek Wall and Orchard Cove.
